To ensure accurate and easy reading, the gauge's top opening is deliberately wider than the inner measuring tube. This difference in diameter acts as an amplifier. A siphon transfers water between two containers by utilizing gravity and atmospheric pressure to move liquid over an elevated barrier. The process begins when the tube is filled with water, creating a continuous column. Gravity pulls the water down the longer, descending leg of the tube toward the lower container. This downward movement creates a partial vacuum or reduced pressure at the top of the siphon. Atmospheric pressure pushing on the surface of the source water then forces more liquid up the shorter leg to fill this low-pressure zone, sustaining the flow.

The outlet must be positioned lower than the source water surface because the driving force is the weight difference between the water columns in the two legs. If the outlet were higher or level with the source, gravity would not pull the water down with sufficient force to overcome the upward lift required on the intake side. This break equalizes the pressure inside the tube with the outside atmosphere, stopping the pressure differential that drives the flow. Consequently, the siphon fails until the tube is re-primed and filled entirely with liquid again.

Jrs don't need tickets or documentation or meeting. They need to sit in on design conversations. They need to see how others debug issues.
